prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "ASML HOLDING NV" (ticker ASML). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:
{"summaries": { "<framework id>": "2-3 plain sentences on how well the company fits this investor's approach, written neutrally" } for EVERY framework below:
   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)
   "lynch": Peter Lynch (“One Up on Wall Street” and “Beating the Street”)
   "fisher": Philip Fisher (“Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits” (the 15 points, condensed))
   "graham": Benjamin Graham (“The Intelligent Investor”, criteria for the defensive investor)
   "thiel": Peter Thiel (“Zero to One”: the seven questions every business must answer)
   "gerstner": Brad Gerstner (His public letters (e.g. “Time to Get Fit”, 2022) and interviews (BG2 podcast); a summary, not an official checklist)
   "druckenmiller": Stanley Druckenmiller (His public interviews and speeches; a summary, not an official checklist)
   "smith": Terry Smith (Fundsmith owner's manual and annual letters (“buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing”))
   "greenblatt": Joel Greenblatt (“The Little Book That Beats the Market” (the Magic Formula))
   "akre": Chuck Akre (Akre's “three-legged stool”)
   "pabrai": Mohnish Pabrai (“The Dhandho Investor”)
   "wood": Cathie Wood (ARK Invest's published research (“Big Ideas”) on disruptive innovation)
   "ackman": Bill Ackman (Pershing Square's stated investment criteria (annual letters and presentations))
   "sleep": Nick Sleep (Nomad Investment Partnership letters (2001–2014))
   "valentine": Don Valentine (His talks (e.g. Stanford GSB, 2010) on what Sequoia looks for)
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM"}

summaries.gardner: ASML fits Gardner's Rule Breaker idea well in most respects: it is the sole supplier of EUV lithography, the key enabler of AI-era chips, with a hard-to-copy advantage, strong momentum (shares up about 83% in a year) and a valuation many call rich. It is less of a fit as a consumer-facing household name and as an emerging company, since it is a mature Dutch firm founded in 1984.
summaries.buffett: ASML has the durable moat, high returns on capital (ROIC around 66%) and strong cash generation Buffett prizes, plus conservative finances. The business is technically complex and tied to the semiconductor cycle, and at about 53 times trailing and 30 times forward earnings it offers little margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would admire ASML as a near-monopoly built on decades of hard-won know-how and an exclusive partnership with Zeiss, a 'great business at a fair price' candidate. Inverting, the main failure paths are export-control and geopolitical shocks, chip-capex downturns and customer concentration, and the high price is the biggest concern.
summaries.lynch: ASML is a cyclical fast grower: 2025 sales rose 15.6% to €32.7 billion and 2026 guidance is €43-45 billion. Lynch would like the simple story (only maker of EUV machines) but would worry that a forward P/E of about 30 versus long-run growth in the teens is not cheap, and that cyclical stocks look cheapest at the wrong time.
summaries.fisher: ASML scores very highly on Fisher's points: decades of R&D (€4.7 billion in 2025) that produced EUV and High-NA EUV, a clear product roadmap to Hyper-NA, close customer relationships and margins rising toward a 56-60% 2030 target. Its main Fisher weakness is dependence on a handful of customers.
summaries.graham: ASML passes Graham's tests for financial strength, size and an unbroken profit record, but fails on price: a trailing P/E of about 53 and price-to-book of about 26 are far above his limits, and its dividend record, though rising, is shorter than 20 years.
summaries.thiel: ASML is close to Thiel's ideal monopoly: it alone makes EUV machines, technology roughly two decades in development that no rival has matched, with timing aligned to AI chip demand. Its durability rests on process know-how, an exclusive optics supply chain and a high-value service business.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner favours durable compounders riding big platform shifts like AI at reasonable prices. ASML is a direct AI beneficiary with accelerating growth (2026 guidance up about 35% at the midpoint) and record bookings, but after an 83% one-year rise the valuation of about 30 times forward earnings demands continued strong execution.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller looks for accelerating earnings and upward estimate revisions, and ASML currently shows both: 2026 sales guidance was raised to €43-45 billion and Q2 2026 gross margin reached 54.0%. The risks to watch are China export rules and any slowdown in chipmakers' capex.
summaries.smith: ASML fits Terry Smith's quality criteria: high gross margin (52.8% in 2025, guided 54-56% for 2026), very high returns on capital and good cash conversion. The question is valuation, with a free-cash-flow yield under 2%.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula ASML's return on capital is outstanding (ROIC about 66%), but its earnings yield is low: EV/EBIT of about 45 implies roughly a 2.2% yield. It would rank high on quality and low on cheapness.
summaries.akre: ASML fits Akre's three-legged stool well: an extraordinary business, capable and engineering-led management under CEO Christophe Fouquet, and ample room to reinvest in EUV capacity and High-NA. The high price would be the main hesitation.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai's Dhandho approach seeks low-risk, high-uncertainty bargains. ASML is low risk in terms of business durability but is not distressed or cheap after an 83% one-year gain, so it does not fit his bargain-hunting style today.
summaries.wood: ASML is an enabler of ARK's AI and robotics themes rather than a disruptive innovator in its own right, but its lithography roadmap is what keeps chip costs falling. ARK typically prefers faster-growing, earlier-stage companies with exponential cost curves.
summaries.ackman: ASML fits Ackman's criteria for simple-to-describe, predictable-over-time, cash-generative businesses with very high barriers to entry and a strong balance sheet. Its cyclicality and the high valuation leave less room for the large upside he looks for.
summaries.sleep: Sleep's 'scale economics shared' model fits partly: each new ASML machine generation lowers the cost per transistor for customers even as ASML raises system prices, and the growing installed base feeds services. It is a long-term, patient-ownership type of business that Nomad's style would appreciate.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge markets and technology that solves a big problem; ASML's EUV is exactly the bottleneck technology that the whole semiconductor industry depends on. As a mature public company rather than a start-up, it fits his venture lens only loosely.

momentum.evidence: ASML's US shares rose 83.5% over the 52 weeks to 13 October 2026 (to $1,717.76), far ahead of the S&P 500's 20.4% total return (SPY).

g4.evidence: It is led by Christophe Fouquet, who ran the EUV business, and partners with Carl Zeiss (exclusive EUV optics) and leading chipmakers TSMC, Samsung and Intel, which co-funded EUV in 2012.

g6.evidence: At about 53 times trailing and 30 times forward earnings, commentators often call ASML expensive, though most analysts still rate it a buy.

simple.evidence: The business model is easy to state (selling and servicing chip-printing machines), but the technology and the semiconductor cycle are hard for a generalist to judge.

b2.evidence: Sales rose every year from €18.6 billion (2021) to €32.7 billion (2025), but operating income dipped in 2022 and 2024, reflecting chip-cycle swings.

integrity.evidence: ASML is known for clear guidance and long-term targets (2030 sales of €44-60 billion), returns capital through dividends and buybacks, and has a Dutch two-tier board structure.

b6.evidence: It stays focused on lithography, metrology and services rather than buying unrelated businesses; its main investment, 24.9% of Carl Zeiss SMT, secures its critical supply chain.

roic.evidence: ROIC is about 66% and ROE about 54% (StockAnalysis, Oct 2026), with little reliance on debt.

fcf.evidence: Operating cash flow was €12,659 million in 2025 on net income of €9,609 million, and trailing free cash flow is about $11.25 billion.

b10.evidence: Retained earnings funded EUV and High-NA development that took ASML from €18.6 billion of sales in 2021 to €32.7 billion in 2025, and its market value is now over $600 billion.

safety.evidence: With a trailing P/E of about 53, P/B of about 26 and a free-cash-flow yield of 1.7%, the price is well above a conservative estimate of value.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of about 30 is high but could be reasonable if 2026 sales reach the guided €43-45 billion and growth continues toward the 2030 targets.

mu5.evidence: Its monopoly in EUV is hard to dislodge, but export controls, a deep chip-capex downturn or dependence on a few customers could hurt it badly.

reinvest.evidence: It keeps expanding EUV capacity (about 65 low-NA EUV systems planned for 2026) and developing High-NA and Hyper-NA EUV, with very high returns on capital.

ly2.evidence: It is a fast grower with a simple story: the only company making EUV machines that every advanced chip needs.

ly3.evidence: A trailing P/E of about 53 and forward P/E of about 30 are well above its expected long-term earnings growth rate.

runway.evidence: ASML targets 2030 sales of €44-60 billion, driven by AI chips, High-NA EUV adoption and a growing service base.

ly7.evidence: The company is reducing its share count (down about 1.4% over the past year through buybacks), but insider ownership is only about 0.01% with no notable insider buying.

ly8.evidence: ASML is one of the most widely followed technology stocks in the world.

fi2.evidence: As low-NA EUV matures it is ramping High-NA EXE systems (four revenue systems in 2025) and researching Hyper-NA.

fi3.evidence: Its R&D (€4.7 billion in 2025) produced EUV, the only tool able to make leading-edge chips, plus High-NA EUV and a 1,000-watt EUV light source in 2025.

fi4.evidence: It works closely with a few large customers and won an 88% customer satisfaction score in 2025, but its sales success comes mainly from having no alternative product.

longterm.evidence: It spends heavily on long-horizon R&D and capacity and sets 2030 targets rather than managing for the next quarter.

gr1.evidence: ASML had €32.7 billion of sales in 2025 and an enterprise value of about $643 billion.

ni10.evidence: ASML has been profitable in every one of the last ten years, with net income rising to €9,609 million in 2025.

gr4.evidence: ASML has paid and generally raised an annual dividend (€7.50 a share for 2025), but its dividend record is shorter than 20 years.

eps10.evidence: EPS was €24.71 in 2025, 72% above 2021's €14.34 alone and several times its mid-2010s level.

gr6.evidence: At about 53 times trailing earnings the share price is far above 15 times average earnings.

gr7.evidence: A P/E of about 53 times a P/B of about 26 gives well over 1,000, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: For the most advanced chip layers, EUV is effectively infinitely better than alternatives because no other company can make an EUV scanner.

timing.evidence: AI chip demand is driving record bookings and 2026 sales guidance of €43-45 billion, up from €32.7 billion in 2025.

th3.evidence: It started by winning the early EUV niche and now expands from it into High-NA, metrology and services.

team.evidence: Management has a strong engineering record, with CEO Fouquet (a physicist-engineer) having led the EUV business before becoming CEO in 2024.

th5.evidence: It sells directly to a handful of chipmakers with deep engineering ties and services the installed base, a powerful route to customers.

durable.evidence: Leading-edge chips will need EUV for at least the next decade and no rival is close, though export controls and alternative patterning are risks.

th7.evidence: ASML saw early that EUV could work when Nikon and Canon gave up, but that insight is now widely recognised.

trend.evidence: It is a key beneficiary of the AI build-out because every leading-edge AI chip from TSMC, Samsung and Intel is patterned on its EUV machines.

dr1.evidence: 2026 sales guidance was raised to €43-45 billion with gross margin of 54-56%, and Q2 2026 gross margin reached 54.0%.

dr2.evidence: High-NA adoption and EUV capacity growth should improve results, but much of this is already expected given the 83% one-year rise.

dr4.evidence: Strong AI-driven chip investment helps, but its sales are cyclical and sensitive to chipmakers' financing conditions and global trade policy.

dr6.evidence: Catalysts include quarterly bookings, High-NA orders, TSMC and Samsung capex plans and possible changes in export rules.

dr7.evidence: Its monopoly supports high conviction, but valuation and cyclicality argue against an outsized position at today's price.

gm.evidence: Gross margin was 52.8% in 2025 and 54.0% in Q2 2026, very high for an equipment maker.

fcfyield.evidence: The free-cash-flow yield is only about 1.7% (P/FCF about 58), demanding for its growth.

gb2.evidence: EV/EBIT is about 45, an earnings yield of only about 2.2% on enterprise value.

pa2.evidence: ASML is not in a setback; demand and the share price are near record highs.

pa4.evidence: Its monopoly position and strong balance sheet make permanent business loss unlikely, though a high price means investors could still lose money.

wo1.evidence: It is a critical enabler of AI rather than an AI company, supplying the machines that make AI chips.

wo2.evidence: Each EUV generation cuts customers' cost per transistor, but ASML's own system prices rise rather than fall.

wo3.evidence: It is focused on lithography and related metrology rather than combining several innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Its market should grow strongly (2030 sales target €44-60 billion versus €32.7 billion in 2025), but not to many times its current size in five years.

ac3.evidence: It is little exposed to commodities but very exposed to export controls, US-China tensions and the chip investment cycle.

ns1.evidence: Higher-productivity machines lower customers' cost per wafer, but ASML keeps much of the gain through higher prices and rising margins.

ns4.evidence: With High-NA EUV ramping and no competitor in sight, its position in 10-20 years looks at least as strong as today.

va2.evidence: It solves the huge problem of printing ever-smaller chip features, which the entire semiconductor and AI industries depend on.
